The raf' is also permissible, by supposing a hidden subject, 'it is guidance and mercy,' and with the meaning, 'These are guidance and mercy.'" The explanation of the opening of this surah has already been given [al-Baqarah: 1-5], up to His saying: ﴿And among people is one who purchases idle talk﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: "This verse was revealed concerning a man who bought a singing slave-girl." Mujāhid said: "It was revealed concerning the buying of singing-girls and female singers." Ibn al-Sāʾib and Muqātil said: "It was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, because he used to be a merchant traveling to Persia, and he would buy the news of the non-Arabs and narrate it to Quraysh, saying to them: 'Muḥammad narrates to you the story of ʿĀd and Thamūd, and I narrate to you the story of Rustam and Isfandiyar and the reports of the Kings of Persia.' So they would find his talk pleasant and would abandon listening to the Qur'an, and so this verse was revealed concerning him."

Regarding the meaning of "idle talk" (lahw al-ḥadīth) there are four opinions:

The first: it is singing. Ibn Masʿūd used to say: "It is singing, by Allah, besides whom there is no god," repeating it three times. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah and Qatādah said likewise. Ibn Abī Najīḥ narrated from Mujāhid that he said: "Lahw is the drum."

The second: that it is whatever distracts from Allah. This was said by al-Ḥasan, and it is narrated from him the same as the first opinion.

The third: that it is shirk (associating partners with Allah). This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The fourth: that it is falsehood. This was said by ʿAṭāʾ.

Regarding the meaning of ﴿purchases﴾ (yashtarī) there are two opinions:

One: he purchases with his wealth, and the story of al-Naḍr supports this. The second: he chooses and prefers it. This was said by Qatādah and Maṭar.

These things are called "idle talk" only because they distract from the remembrance of Allah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿to mislead﴾ (liyuḍilla, لِيُضِلَّ). The meaning is: so that his affair ends in misguidance. We have already explained this word in [al-Ḥajj: 9].

Abū Razīn, al-Ḥasan, Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif, al-Aʿmash and Abū Jaʿfar recited it as "liyuḍilla" (لِيُضِلَّ) with a ḍammah on the yāʾ, meaning: so that he misleads others. When he misleads others, he himself also goes astray.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and take them in ridicule﴾ (wa-yattakhidhahā, وَيَتَّخِذَها). Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim recited it as "wa-yattakhidhu" (وَيَتَّخِذُ) with a ḍammah on the dhāl. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim recited it with a fatḥah on the dhāl. Abū ʿAlī said: "Whoever recites with the naṣb has made it coordinate with 'liyuḍilla' (so that he misleads) and 'wa-yattakhidha' (and takes), and whoever recites with the raf' has made it coordinate with 'man yashtarī' (whoever purchases) and 'wa-yattakhidhu' (and takes)."

Regarding what is referred to by the pronoun in ﴿them﴾ (wa-yattakhidhahā), there are two opinions: one, that it refers to the verses; the second, that it refers to the way (sabīl).

What follows this has been explained in several places already [al-Isrāʾ: 46; al-Anʿām: 25; al-Baqarah: 25; al-Raʿd: 2; al-Naḥl: 15; al-Shuʿarāʾ: 7], up to His saying: ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾. Regarding it there are two opinions: one, that it is understanding and intellect, said by most scholars; the second, that it is prophethood. Scholars differ regarding his prophethood, with two opinions:

One: he was a sage but not a prophet. This was said by Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, Mujāhid and Qatādah.

The second: he was a prophet. This was said by al-Shaʿbī, ʿIkrimah and al-Suddī. This is how al-Wāḥidī reported it from them, and it is not well known, except that this is something ʿIkrimah alone reported. The first opinion is more sound.

Regarding his occupation there are three opinions: one, that he was a tailor, said by Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib; the second, that he was a shepherd, said by Ibn Zayd; the third, that he was a carpenter, said by Khālid al-Rabaʿī.

As for his description, Ibn ʿAbbās said: "He was an Abyssinian slave." Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib said: "Luqman was one of the blacks of Egypt, very dark." Mujāhid said: "He had thick lips and cracked feet, and he was a judge over the Children of Israel."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Be grateful to Allah﴾ (an ushkur lillāh). The meaning: We said to him, "Be grateful to Allah [for] what He has given you of wisdom." ﴿And whoever is grateful, is only grateful for [the benefit of] himself﴾, i.e., he only does it for his own self. ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ the blessing, then indeed Allah is Free of need from the worship of His creation.

(p-319) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man (concerning) his parents﴾. Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. We have explained this in (al-'Ankabut: 8).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness﴾. al-Dahhak and Asim al-Jahdari recited: "wahnan 'ala wahnin" with a fatha on the ha' in both. al-Zajjaj said: That is, weakness upon weakness. The meaning is: her carrying him obliged her to grow weak time after time. The place of "an" (that) is in the accusative governed by "wassayna" (We enjoined); the meaning is: "And We enjoined upon man that he give thanks to Me and to your parents," that is, We enjoined him to give thanks to Us and to his parents.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And his weaning is in two years﴾. That is, his weaning takes place at the end of two years. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Abu 'Imran and al-A'mash recited: "wa fisaluhu" with a fatha on the fa'. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Talha ibn Musarrif, Asim al-Jahdari and Qatada recited: "wa fasluhu" with a fatha on the fa' and a sukun on the sad, without an alif. The purpose is to draw attention to the hardship of the mother in nursing after carrying.

(p-320) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they both strive with you﴾. **Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 31, verses 20–21:**

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And He has lavished upon you﴾, meaning: He extended and perfected ﴿His favours﴾ (نِعَمَهُ). Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 31, verses 22–27:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever submits his face﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu al-'Aliyah, and Qatadah recited "wa-man yusallim" with a fathah on the sin and a shaddah on the lam. The exegetes mentioned that His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, let not his disbelief grieve you﴾ is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword, but this is not sound, because it is a consolation against grief, and that does not contradict the command to fight. As for what follows this, the explanation of its words has already preceded in several places [Hud: 48; al-'Ankabut: 61; al-Baqarah: 267], down to His saying: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾. Regarding its occasion of revelation there are two views.

One of them: "The rabbis of the Jews said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Have you considered the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra': 85]; does He mean us, or your people?' He said: 'No.' They said: 'Do you not recite in what has come to you that we have been given the Torah, in which is an explanation of everything?' He said: 'Indeed it is, in the knowledge of Allah, little.' So this verse was revealed." Narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: The polytheists said about the Qur'an: "It is only words that will soon be exhausted and cut off," so this verse was revealed. Said by Qatadah.

The meaning of the verse: Even if the trees of the earth were pens, and the sea, with seven more seas beside it, were ink — and in the speech there is an omitted element, its estimate being: "then the words of Allah were written with these pens and these seas" — the pens would break and the seas would be exhausted, and the words of Allah would not be exhausted, meaning they would not be cut off.

As for His saying: ﴿And the sea﴾, Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited "wal-bahru" with a dammah (raf'), while Abu 'Amr read it with a fathah (nasb). Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads "wal-bahra" with a fathah, it is conjoined to "ma" (in "ma fi al-ardi"); the meaning: "Even if whatever is on the earth, and even if the sea..." The raf' is good according to the sense: "and the sea, this is its condition." Al-Yazidi said: The meaning of ﴿yamudduhu min ba'dihi﴾ is: it increases it; one says: "Mudda qidraka," i.e., add to its water. Likewise Ibn Qutaybah said: "yamuddu-hu" is from al-midad (ink), not from al-imdad (provision); one says: "I replenished my inkwell with ink (madadtu dawati bil-midad), and I supplied him with wealth and men (amdadtuhu bil-mal wal-rijal)."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 31, verses 28–32:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only like that of a single soul﴾. The occasion of its revelation: Ubayy ibn Khalaf, along with others from the Quraysh, said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah created us in stages: a drop of semen, a clinging clot, a lump of flesh, bones, then flesh. Then you claim that we will be resurrected as a new creation, all together in a single hour?!" So this verse was revealed. Its meaning: Your creation, O people, all of you, in terms of power, is only like the creation of a single soul, and your resurrection, all of you, in terms of power, is only like the resurrection of a single soul. This was said by Muqatil.

As for what follows, its tafsir has already been given (Al 'Imran: 27; al-Ra'd: 2; al-Hajj: 62), up to His saying: ﴿Do you not see that the ships sail upon the sea by the favor of Allah?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: among His favors is the sailing of the ships. ﴿That He may show you of His signs﴾, meaning: that He may show you of His handiwork His wonders (p-328) in the sea, and [in] seeking provision. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful [person]﴾. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 31, verses 33–34:

(p-329) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾. The exegetes said: This is an address to the disbelievers of Makkah. His saying: ﴿No father will avail anything for his child﴾, meaning he will not settle on his behalf any part of his crimes and wrongdoings. Muqatil said: By this he means the disbelievers. We have explained this in (al-Baqarah: 48). Al-Zajjaj said: His saying: ﴿Nor is a son at all to avail his father﴾, the word "jaz" (ﻫُﻮَ جازٍ) was written in the codices without a yā'. The original form is "jaziyun" with a ḍammah and tanwin. Sibawayh and al-Khalil mentioned that the preferred pausal form is "jaz" without a yā', and thus the eloquent Arabs paused, to make known that this yā' drops in connected speech. Yunus claimed that some trustworthy Arabs pause with a yā', but the preferred practice is to follow the codex.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾, meaning, of resurrection and recompense. ﴿So let not the worldly life delude you﴾ with its adornments, away from Islam and from provisioning oneself for the Hereafter. ﴿Nor let the Deceiver deceive you about Allah﴾, meaning, through His forbearance and His reprieve. ﴿The Deceiver (al-Gharur)﴾ means: Satan, the one whose nature it is to deceive. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-Gharur" is on the pattern of "fa'ul", and "fa'ul" is among the intensive forms (ism al-mubalaghah). It is said: "Fulan akul" when he eats a great deal, and "darub" when he strikes a great deal; so Satan was called "gharur" because he deceives greatly. Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-Gharur" with a fatḥah on the ghayn means Satan, and with a ḍammah means falsehood.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "A man from (p-330) the people of the desert came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: My wife is pregnant, so inform me what she will bear. Our land is barren, so inform me when the rain will fall. I know when I was born, so inform me when I will die. Then this verse was revealed." Related by Mujahid.

The meaning of the verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿has knowledge of the Hour﴾, when it will occur; no one other than Him knows that. ﴿And He sends down the rain﴾. Nafi', Asim and Ibn 'Amir recited "wa-yunazzilu" with shaddah, so no one knows when the rain will fall, by night or by day. ﴿And He knows what is in the wombs﴾: no one other than Him knows what is in them, whether male or female, white or black. ﴿And no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow﴾, whether good or evil. ﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾, meaning in what place. Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "bi-ayyati ardin" with a kasrah on the tā'. The meaning: no one knows [where] his resting place on the earth will be until he dies, whether on land, sea, plain or mountain. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "bi-ayyi ardin kunta" and "bi-ayyati ardin kunta" are two dialects. Al-Farra' said: whoever says "bi-ayyi ardin" uses the feminine of "ard" and so does not need to show a second feminine marker in "ayy". Ibn 'Abbas said: No close angel and no sent prophet knows these five. Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever claims to know any of these has disbelieved in the Qur'an, because he has contradicted it.
